title: Block close: many rooms
hook: the family disagrees, and still says one creed

segments.voice: Yesterday, in essentials, unity, and an old motto that ends in love. Your line was in all things, charity. Which disagreement did you hold more kindly? Day one thousand one hundred eleven.

A family can share one house and still argue about the thermostat, the dishes, whose turn it is to cook. Through this whole block of the path, the Christian family has been arguing out loud: about the table, about Mary, about the saints, about images and the dead. No church here was asked to back down, and none did. And yet the Nicene Creed, said in Orthodox, Catholic and other churches, still opens with the same words: I believe in one God. Today the block closes. Today's word: block close.

This block asked the big questions, and let each church answer in its own voice. It began with words about God: theology, and the way of not-knowing that says what God is not. It asked where authority lives, sola scriptura, scripture alone, or scripture read within the church's tradition, and what it means to call scripture God-breathed. It tried pictures of the Trinity that all fall short, and the filioque, one word in a long argument. Then sin and grace: Augustine and Pelagius, the Reformed comfort of being chosen, Wesley's grace that goes before. The cross from several sides: victory over death, a debt paid, a place taken, a love that changes us. Justified by faith. Made holy. Theosis, becoming like God, iron glowing in the fire. Then the church itself: its marks, its ministers, its water and its table. Mary, the God-bearer. The saints, the images, the dead. Heaven, hell, and the promise of his return. The answers differed, and this block didn't pretend otherwise. But listen to Jesus on his last night, praying for everyone who would believe through his friends: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee." And earlier that same evening, to friends who were frightened: "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you." Mansions, in the King James. Dwelling places. Rooms. Many of them, in one house, and room enough for a family that argues.

Here's the practice: pray for someone who believes differently. Let yourself settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose faith isn't yours. A Christian from another church. A neighbor from another tradition. A friend who holds no faith. Don't think about where you disagree. Think about their face, their week, what they might be carrying. If you pray, you can ask good things for them, in words your tradition gives you. If you don't, just wish them peace, warmly. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of the big questions: many answers, honestly different, from one family that still says one creed. Tomorrow a new block begins: traditions of prayer.
Your line: many rooms, one house. Today, learn one thing from a Christian of another church, or a neighbor of another faith, and say thank you. Day one thousand one hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches say the Nicene Creed in their worship, and Christians of different churches pray together, especially in shared services for Christian unity.

fork.setup: it's Jesus's last night with his friends. he prays for them, and for everyone who will believe through them. what does he ask?
options: that they all may be one.
that they never meet anyone different.
fork.reveal: "that they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee." a prayer for a family that would come to disagree.

original.note: Greek: a dwelling place, a place to stay; the word behind "mansions" in John 14:2.

trapdoor: what you thought: agreeing to disagree.
what it means: one family that differs honestly, and still says one creed.
what a scholar hears: the King James "mansions" renders a Greek word for dwelling places: many rooms in one Father's house.

notes: Block close for Block A (days 1062–1111): the teach recaps the block's topics from the outline.
Hook's 'one city' scene (Lutheran, Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican churches saying the Nicene Creed on a Sunday) is illustrative. Lutheran and Anglican use varies by service; confirm.
'I believe in one God' is the Nicene Creed's opening (not marked as a quotation).
John 14 and John 17 are both set on the last night; 'earlier that same evening' assumes the Farewell Discourse's sequence. Confirm.
Original μονή (plural μοναί in John 14:2); confirm.

Editor: rewrote the hook, which repeated day 1096's opener (churches on a Sunday all saying the Nicene Creed) and the 'across town' image used on days 1095 and 1105; it now opens on a family arguing under one roof. The earlier note on the Lutheran/Anglican Sunday scene no longer applies.

Auditor: "a friend who believes nothing at all" softened to "a friend who holds no faith" so non-believing listeners are not belittled. John 17:21 and John 14:2 checked against the KJV; the block recap matches the titles of days 1062–1110.
